krisenjahr-1923#text: When Germany fell behind with its reparation deliveries, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr region in January 1923. The Reich government called for passive resistance and paid the striking workers with freshly printed money, which drove the inflation that had been running since the war to immeasurable heights: in November one dollar cost 4.2 trillion marks, a loaf of bread cost billions, and wages were paid out daily so that they could still be spent on the same day. Gustav Stresemann, chancellor since August, broke off the struggle in the Ruhr and on 15 November introduced the Rentenmark, which stabilized the currency. A few days earlier, on 8 and 9 November, Adolf Hitler had attempted a putsch in Munich together with Erich Ludendorff, which ended in a hail of police bullets in front of the Feldherrnhalle; Hitler used the trial as a stage and wrote his book Mein Kampf in prison.
weltwirtschaftskrise-1929#summary: The stock market crash in New York plunges the world into the most severe economic crisis of modern times.
weltwirtschaftskrise-1929#text: On 24 October 1929, Black Thursday, share prices collapsed on the New York stock exchange. Banks went bankrupt, American loans were withdrawn from Europe, and world trade shrank by more than half. In the United States one in four of the workforce was unemployed in 1933, and in Germany more than six million people were out of work. The hardship undermined confidence in democracy and contributed decisively to the rise of the National Socialists.
salzmarsch-gandhis#summary: With a march of 385 kilometers to the sea, Gandhi breaks the British salt monopoly and makes nonviolent resistance known throughout the world.
salzmarsch-gandhis#text: The British salt monopoly forbade Indians to produce salt themselves and placed a tax on this basic foodstuff that hit the poor hardest. On 12 March 1930 Mohandas Gandhi set out from his ashram near Ahmedabad with 78 followers; after 24 days he reached the village of Dandi on the Arabian Sea accompanied by tens of thousands of people and there, on 6 April, demonstratively picked up a handful of salt. All over the country people now boiled salt, boycotted British goods and resigned from public office; the colonial power arrested more than 60,000 people, Gandhi himself among them. The images of police beating peaceful demonstrators went around the world and weakened the moral authority of the empire. The march became a model for nonviolent movements right up to Martin Luther King.
buecherverbrennung-1933#summary: In Berlin and twenty other university towns, students throw the works of Jewish, left-wing and pacifist authors into the fire.
buecherverbrennung-1933#text: In the spring of 1933 the National Socialist German Students' League called for a campaign against the un-German spirit and ransacked libraries and bookshops. On 10 May 1933 students and SA men burned tens of thousands of books by torchlight on the Opernplatz in Berlin, while propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels proclaimed the end of Jewish intellectualism; similar fires burned in Bonn, Frankfurt, Munich, Dresden and many other cities. Among those affected were Heinrich and Thomas Mann, Erich Kästner, who watched the burning of his own books from the crowd, Kurt Tucholsky, Erich Maria Remarque, Sigmund Freud, Karl Marx and Bertolt Brecht. More than a hundred years earlier Heinrich Heine, whose works also burned, had written that where books are burned, in the end people will be burned too. The burning stood at the beginning of a cultural policy that drove modern literature out of Germany.
machtuebernahme-nationalsozialisten#summ: Hitler becomes chancellor and establishes a dictatorship within a few months.
machtuebernahme-nationalsozialisten#text: On 30 January 1933 Reich President Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor of a coalition in which conservative politicians believed they could control him. After the Reichstag fire, the emergency decree of 28 February suspended fundamental rights, and the Enabling Act of 23 March transferred legislative power to the government. By the summer all other parties had been banned, the trade unions smashed and the first concentration camps set up. After Hindenburg's death in 1934, Hitler combined the offices of chancellor and president as Führer and Reich Chancellor.
reichstagsbrand-und-ermaechtigungsgesetz: The burning of the Reichstag provides the pretext for abolishing fundamental rights; the Enabling Act strips parliament of its power.

On the night of 27 February 1933 the Reichstag building stood in flames; at the scene the Dutch council communist Marinus van der Lubbe was arrested, who claimed to have acted alone. That same night the government declared the fire to be the signal for a communist uprising, and as early as 28 February the Reichstag Fire Decree suspended freedom of opinion, of the press and of assembly as well as protection against arbitrary arrest. Thousands of communists and social democrats were arrested, and the election of 5 March took place under terror. On 23 March, in the Kroll Opera House surrounded by the SA, the Reichstag approved the Enabling Act by 444 votes to 94, allowing the government to issue laws without parliament and without the constitution; only the SPD voted against, and its chairman Otto Wels declared that freedom and life could be taken from them, but not their honor. The KPD deputies had already been arrested or had gone into hiding.
langer-marsch#summary: China's communists escape encirclement by Chiang Kai-shek in a year-long retreat that brings Mao Zedong to the head of the party.
langer-marsch#text: From 1927 onward Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist Chinese government fought the communists, who had established a soviet republic of their own in the southern Chinese province of Jiangxi. When the fifth encirclement campaign threatened to crush the Red Army in the autumn of 1934, some 86,000 soldiers and cadres broke out to the west. Crossing rivers, swamps and snow-covered mountains, they covered several thousand kilometers in one year, constantly pursued by government troops and local warlords; only a few thousand reached the region around Yan'an in northern China in October 1935. At the Zunyi Conference in January 1935 Mao Zedong had taken over the leadership. The Long March became a founding myth of the People's Republic, and after the Xi'an Incident in 1936 Chiang and the communists had to form a united front against Japan.
nuernberger-gesetze#summary: The racial laws make Jews second-class citizens and prohibit marriages with non-Jews.
nuernberger-gesetze#text: At the party rally in Nuremberg on 15 September 1935, the Reichstag proclaimed the Reich Citizenship Law and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honor. Jews lost their full civil rights, and marriages and relationships between Jews and non-Jews were made punishable. Who counted as a Jew was decided by the authorities on the basis of the origin of the grandparents, not on the basis of faith. The laws created the legal basis for the exclusion, expropriation and later deportation of the Jews.
grosse-saeuberung#title: Great Purge in the Soviet Union
grosse-saeuberung#summary: In show trials and mass operations Stalin has hundreds of thousands shot as alleged enemies of the people.
grosse-saeuberung#text: After the murder of the Leningrad party leader Sergei Kirov in December 1934, Stalin used the fear of conspiracies to destroy every actual or possible opposition. In three Moscow show trials between 1936 and 1938, old companions of Lenin such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin confessed under torture to invented crimes and were shot; Trotsky, who had been driven into exile, was also condemned in absentia and murdered in Mexico in 1940. In 1937 Stalin had the leadership of the Red Army around Marshal Tukhachevsky executed. In the mass operations of the NKVD secret police under Nikolai Yezhov, around 750,000 people were shot according to quotas in 1937 and 1938, and well over a million were deported to the camps of the Gulag. The purge destroyed the country's leading stratum and weakened the army shortly before the German attack.
spanischer-buergerkrieg#summary: Nationalists under Franco overthrow the Spanish republic with German and Italian help.
spanischer-buergerkrieg#text: In July 1936 parts of the military under General Francisco Franco rose against the elected government of the Popular Front. Germany and Italy sent aircraft and troops, the Soviet Union supported the republic, and volunteers from all over the world fought in the International Brigades. The destruction of the Basque town of Guernica by the German Condor Legion in 1937 became a symbol of aerial warfare against civilians. Franco's victory in April 1939 established a dictatorship that lasted until 1975.
nanking-massaker#summary: After capturing the Chinese capital, Japanese troops commit mass murder and mass rape for weeks on end.
nanking-massaker#text: Since the Marco Polo Bridge Incident in July 1937 Japan had waged open war against China, and after heavy fighting around Shanghai it took the capital Nanking on 13 December 1937. Over the following six weeks Japanese soldiers shot, stabbed and drowned tens of thousands of captured soldiers and civilians, raped tens of thousands of women and girls, and looted and burned the city. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East assumed more than 200,000 dead, and China gives the figure of 300,000; historians dispute the number, but not the crime. A group of foreigners around the German Siemens representative John Rabe set up a safety zone in which around 200,000 people found protection. The massacre still burdens relations between China and Japan today, because Japanese nationalists play it down or deny it.
muenchner-abkommen#summary: Britain and France hand Hitler the Sudetenland in order to avoid war; Czechoslovakia is not consulted.
muenchner-abkommen#text: After the annexation of Austria in March 1938, Hitler demanded the cession of the Sudetenland, the border regions of Czechoslovakia inhabited by around three million Germans, and threatened war. The British prime minister Neville Chamberlain flew to Germany three times to negotiate, and during the night of 30 September 1938 Hitler, Mussolini, Chamberlain and the French prime minister Daladier signed the agreement in Munich, which laid down that the cession was to take place within ten days. The Czechoslovak government, allied with France, had to give in and lost its border fortifications. In London people cheered Chamberlain, who promised peace for our time; Winston Churchill called the agreement a total defeat. In March 1939 the Wehrmacht occupied the remainder of the Czech lands and demonstrated that the policy of appeasement had failed.
novemberpogrome-1938#summary: During the night of 9 to 10 November, synagogues burn throughout the Reich and Jewish businesses are destroyed.
novemberpogrome-1938#text: The pretext was the assassination of a German diplomat in Paris by a young Jew. On Goebbels's instructions, the SA and SS destroyed more than 1,400 synagogues and thousands of businesses and homes, and hundreds of people were killed. Around 30,000 Jewish men were deported to concentration camps. The victims had to pay for the damage themselves and to raise an atonement payment of one billion reichsmarks. The pogroms marked the transition from the removal of rights to open violence.
hitler-stalin-pakt#summary: The mortal enemies Germany and the Soviet Union conclude a non-aggression pact and secretly divide Eastern Europe between them.
hitler-stalin-pakt#text: On 23 August 1939 the foreign ministers Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov signed a non-aggression treaty in Moscow that took the world by surprise, because National Socialism and communism had fought each other for years as arch-enemies. A secret additional protocol divided Poland along the rivers Narew, Vistula and San and assigned Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Bessarabia to the Soviet sphere of interest and Lithuania initially to the German one. Hitler thereby had a free hand for the attack on Poland, while Stalin gained time and territory. In September 1939 the Soviet Union occupied eastern Poland, in the spring of 1940 had around 22,000 Polish officers and officials shot at Katyn, waged war against Finland and annexed the Baltic states in 1940. The Soviet Union denied the existence of the protocol until 1989.
ueberfall-auf-polen#title: Invasion of Poland and the Outbreak of War
ueberfall-auf-polen#summary: With the German attack on Poland on 1 September 1939 the Second World War begins.
ueberfall-auf-polen#text: One week after the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, which in a secret additional protocol divided Poland between Germany and the Soviet Union, the Wehrmacht attacked without a declaration of war. Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September, but were unable to help Poland. On 17 September the Red Army marched in from the east; by the beginning of October Poland was defeated. In the occupied territories the mass shootings of the Polish leading class and the persecution of the Jews began at once.
luftschlacht-um-england#summary: The Royal Air Force prevents the Luftwaffe from gaining air supremacy and thereby prevents the German invasion of Britain.
luftschlacht-um-england#text: After the fall of France, Britain stood alone, and Hitler had a landing on the English coast prepared, for which the Royal Air Force first had to be eliminated. From July to October 1940 the Luftwaffe attacked ports, airfields and radar stations, but the British Spitfire and Hurricane fighters, guided by the radar system and the ground control of Fighter Command, inflicted heavier losses on the attackers than they suffered themselves; pilots from Poland, Czechoslovakia, Canada and other countries fought alongside them. When the Luftwaffe switched in September to night attacks on London and other cities, the Blitz, this gave the Royal Air Force the decisive respite. On 17 September Hitler postponed the invasion indefinitely; by May 1941 more than 40,000 British civilians had died in the bombing war. Churchill thanked the pilots with the words that never was so much owed by so many to so few.
westfeldzug-1940#title: Western Campaign and the Fall of France
westfeldzug-1940#summary: In six weeks the Wehrmacht defeats the Netherlands, Belgium and France; de Gaulle calls for resistance from London.
westfeldzug-1940#text: On 10 May 1940 the Wehrmacht attacked the neutral Netherlands and Belgium and, with its panzer divisions, among them the 7th Panzer Division led by Erwin Rommel, pushed unexpectedly through the wooded Ardennes, where the Allies did not expect an attack. Within a week the Germans reached the Channel coast and cut off the British and French armies in Belgium; around 338,000 soldiers were evacuated across the Channel at Dunkirk. Paris fell on 14 June, and on 22 June the new government under Marshal Pétain signed the capitulation in the same railway carriage at Compiègne in which the armistice had been sealed in 1918; northern France was occupied, and in the south the Vichy regime arose, which collaborated with Germany. On 18 June General Charles de Gaulle called on the French over the BBC to continue the fight; out of his Free France and the networks of the Résistance inside the country there grew by 1944 a resistance movement that carried out sabotage, hid the persecuted and supplied the Allies with information.
angriff-auf-die-sowjetunion#summary: With Operation Barbarossa the German war of annihilation in the east begins on 22 June 1941.
angriff-auf-die-sowjetunion#text: More than three million German and allied soldiers crossed the border into the Soviet Union; it was the largest attack in military history. The aim was the conquest of living space and the destruction of Bolshevism. Behind the front, Einsatzgruppen shot hundreds of thousands of Jews, Soviet prisoners of war were left to starve to death in their millions, and the siege of Leningrad cost more than a million civilians their lives. The advance came to a halt before Moscow in December 1941.
angriff-auf-pearl-harbor#summary: Japan launches a surprise attack on the American Pacific Fleet in Hawaii; the United States enters the war.
angriff-auf-pearl-harbor#text: On 7 December 1941 Japanese carrier aircraft sank or damaged eight battleships and killed more than 2,400 Americans. Japan wanted to secure its expansion in Southeast Asia after the United States had imposed an oil embargo. On the following day Congress declared war on Japan, and a few days later Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. With that the war had definitively become a world war, and the industrial superiority of the United States began to take effect.
schlacht-um-midway#summary: The US Navy sinks four Japanese aircraft carriers and halts Japanese expansion in the Pacific.
schlacht-um-midway#text: Six months after Pearl Harbor, Admiral Yamamoto sought to force the American fleet into a decisive battle by attacking the atoll of Midway. American codebreakers, however, had partly deciphered the Japanese naval code, so that Admiral Nimitz was able to position his three carriers in ambush. On 4 June 1942 American dive bombers hit the Japanese carriers at the very moment when their aircraft were being refueled and armed on deck; Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu sank, and the United States lost the Yorktown. Japan lost the core of its carrier fleet and hundreds of experienced pilots and was never able to replace these losses, while American shipyards delivered new ships every month. From Guadalcanal onward in August 1942 the United States went on the offensive in the Pacific.
schlacht-von-el-alamein#summary: The British Eighth Army defeats Rommel's panzer army in Egypt and turns the war in North Africa.
schlacht-von-el-alamein#text: Since 1941 the German Afrika Korps under Erwin Rommel and Italian troops had been fighting the British for Libya and for access to the Suez Canal and the oil fields of the Middle East. In the summer of 1942, after the capture of Tobruk, Rommel stood only 100 kilometers from Alexandria, but his supply lines were overextended, and Allied aircraft and submarines sank his tankers in the Mediterranean. The new British commander Bernard Montgomery attacked on 23 October 1942 with roughly twice the strength in soldiers, tanks and aircraft, including troops from Australia, New Zealand, India and South Africa; after twelve days the German-Italian front broke, and Rommel withdrew to the west in defiance of an order from Hitler to hold. A few days later American and British troops landed in Morocco and Algeria; in May 1943 around 250,000 Axis soldiers surrendered in Tunisia. Churchill called El Alamein the end of the beginning.
schlacht-von-stalingrad#summary: The encirclement and destruction of the Sixth Army on the Volga is regarded as the turning point of the war in Europe.
schlacht-von-stalingrad#text: In the summer of 1942 the Wehrmacht advanced as far as the Volga and fought in bitter street battles for the city of Stalingrad. In November the Red Army encircled the German troops; Hitler forbade a breakout. After hunger, cold and fighting, the remnants of the Sixth Army surrendered on 2 February 1943. About 150,000 German soldiers had been killed and around 90,000 were taken prisoner, of whom only about 6,000 returned. After that the Wehrmacht was permanently on the defensive in the east.
wannseekonferenz#summary: Senior officials and SS leaders coordinate the deportation and murder of all European Jews.
wannseekonferenz#text: On 20 January 1942 fifteen representatives of the SS, the party and the ministries met under the chairmanship of Reinhard Heydrich in a villa on the Wannsee in Berlin. The conference did not decide on the genocide, since mass murder had already been under way for months, but organized the cooperation of the authorities in the so-called Final Solution of the Jewish Question. The minutes named eleven million Jews across the whole of Europe as the target group. In the months that followed, the deportations to the extermination camps of Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau began.
aufstand-im-warschauer-ghetto#summary: The last inhabitants of the ghetto put up armed resistance to the SS for almost four weeks, choosing to fight rather than be deported.
aufstand-im-warschauer-ghetto#text: In the Warsaw ghetto, which the German occupation had sealed off with a wall in 1940, more than 400,000 people lived crammed into the narrowest of spaces, and tens of thousands of them died of hunger and disease. Between July and September 1942 the SS deported about 265,000 inhabitants to the Treblinka extermination camp. The remaining 60,000 or so now knew what deportation meant; young people joined together in the Jewish Combat Organization under the 24-year-old Mordechai Anielewicz and in the Jewish Military Union, laboriously procuring pistols and homemade firebombs. When the SS moved in on 19 April 1943 for the final clearance, it came under fire and had to withdraw. The SS commander Jürgen Stroop thereupon had the ghetto burned down and blown up house by house; on 8 May Anielewicz and his comrades died in the bunker on Miła Street, and on 16 May, after the demolition of the Great Synagogue, Stroop reported that the ghetto no longer existed. About 7,000 people had died in the fighting, and the survivors were deported to Treblinka and Majdanek. The uprising was the first large armed revolt in an occupied city and became a symbol of Jewish resistance.
attentat-vom-20-juli-1944#summary: Stauffenberg's bomb misses Hitler, the coup fails, and the regime takes revenge with hundreds of executions.
attentat-vom-20-juli-1944#text: A circle of officers, diplomats, trade unionists and politicians had been planning for years to remove Hitler and end the war before Germany was completely destroyed. On 20 July 1944 Colonel Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg detonated a bomb in a briefcase during a situation conference at the Wolf's Lair headquarters in East Prussia. Four men died, but Hitler was only slightly injured because the briefcase had been pushed behind a massive table support. Stauffenberg flew to Berlin and, with his fellow conspirators in the Bendlerblock, set in motion the Valkyrie plan, under which the Replacement Army was to take power; when word spread that Hitler had survived, the coup collapsed. Stauffenberg, Friedrich Olbricht, Albrecht Mertz von Quirnheim and Werner von Haeften were shot in the courtyard that same night. In the following months the People's Court under Roland Freisler sentenced around 200 people to death, among them Helmuth James von Moltke, Carl Goerdeler and Julius Leber; their relatives were taken into kin liability detention. Today 20 July is regarded as a symbol of the fact that even among the leading class of the Reich there were people who placed their conscience above obedience.
d-day-normandie#summary: With the largest landing operation in history, the Western Allies open the second front in France.
d-day-normandie#text: On 6 June 1944 more than 150,000 American, British and Canadian soldiers landed on five stretches of beach in Normandy, supported by almost 7,000 ships and 11,000 aircraft. Despite heavy losses, above all at Omaha Beach, a bridgehead was successfully established. By the end of August Paris had been liberated, and the Wehrmacht had to withdraw to the German border. At the same time the Soviet summer offensive smashed the German Army Group Centre.
atombomben-hiroshima-nagasaki#title: Atomic Bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki
atombomben-hiroshima-nagasaki#summary: The United States uses nuclear weapons for the first time; Japan surrenders and the Second World War is over.
atombomben-hiroshima-nagasaki#text: On 6 August 1945 the atomic bomb Little Boy destroyed the city of Hiroshima, and on 9 August Fat Man struck Nagasaki. By the end of 1945 more than 200,000 people had died from the explosion, the fires and the radiation. President Truman wanted to avoid a costly invasion of Japan; at the same time the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. On 15 August Emperor Hirohito announced the surrender, which was signed on 2 September. The atomic age had begun.
befreiung-von-auschwitz#summary: Soviet soldiers reach the largest extermination camp of the National Socialists on 27 January 1945.
befreiung-von-auschwitz#text: At Auschwitz-Birkenau in occupied Poland the SS had murdered more than 1.1 million people between 1940 and 1945, among them around one million Jews, as well as Poles, Sinti and Roma and Soviet prisoners of war. Shortly before the liberation the SS drove about 60,000 prisoners westward on death marches; the soldiers of the Red Army found around 7,000 exhausted survivors, among them many children. Today 27 January is the international day of remembrance for the victims of the Holocaust.
gruendung-vereinte-nationen#summary: 51 states sign the Charter of the United Nations in San Francisco.
gruendung-vereinte-nationen#text: While the war was still going on, the Allies had prepared a new world organization that was to be stronger than the failed League of Nations. The charter was signed on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October. The Security Council, with its five permanent members the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China, received the right to decide on sanctions and military operations. In 1948 the General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
kapitulation-deutschlands-1945#summary: With the unconditional surrender of the Wehrmacht on 8 May 1945 the war in Europe comes to an end.
kapitulation-deutschlands-1945#text: After the Red Army had captured Berlin and Hitler had taken his own life in the bunker of the Reich Chancellery on 30 April, the leadership of the Wehrmacht signed the unconditional surrender on 7 May in Reims and on 8 May in Berlin-Karlshorst. Germany was divided into four occupation zones, and the major war criminals were indicted before the Nuremberg tribunal. In Germany today 8 May is understood as the day of liberation from National Socialism.
nuernberger-prozesse#summary: For the first time the leaders of a state have to answer before an international court for waging a war of aggression and for crimes against humanity.
nuernberger-prozesse#text: In the summer of 1945 the four victorious powers agreed not to shoot those chiefly responsible for the Nazi regime by summary justice, but to charge them in proceedings under the rule of law. From 20 November 1945 to 1 October 1946 the International Military Tribunal sat in the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg and tried 24 defendants, among them Hermann Göring, Rudolf Hess, Joachim von Ribbentrop and Albert Speer, for conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. The evidence consisted above all of the perpetrators' own files, together with films from the liberated camps and testimony from survivors; the objection that they had only been following orders was not accepted as an excuse. Twelve defendants were sentenced to death, Göring escaped execution by taking poison, and three were acquitted. In twelve subsequent trials up to 1949, doctors, lawyers, industrialists, diplomats and commanders of the Einsatzgruppen stood before American courts, and in Tokyo a parallel tribunal tried the Japanese leadership. The Nuremberg Principles became the foundation of international criminal law and of the International Criminal Court.
unabhaengigkeit-indien-pakistan#summary: British India becomes independent and is divided into the states of India and Pakistan.
unabhaengigkeit-indien-pakistan#text: After decades of nonviolent resistance under Mahatma Gandhi, Britain released its most important colony into independence on 15 August 1947. Because Hindus and Muslims could not agree on a common state, the country was divided into predominantly Hindu India and Muslim Pakistan. Up to 15 million people fled across the new borders, and hundreds of thousands died in massacres. The dispute over Kashmir still burdens relations between the two nuclear powers today.
